    #32810. Second Amendment as a Right to Sell Guns as Well as to Have and Buy Them?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2033 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Second Amendment as a Right to Sell Guns as Well as to Have and Buy Them?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho and Andrew Oldham in an unsigned opinion filed yesterday in U.S.
    • Jeremiah Deare was indicted for conspiracy to engage in the business of dealing firearms without a federal firearms license in violation of 18 U.S.C.
    • Recent findings suggest that the district court denied his motion to dismiss, holding that federal licensing and record-keeping requirements are not implicated by the Second Amendment because such requirements do not affect an individual's right to keep or bear arms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho and Andrew Oldham in an unsigned opinion filed yesterday in U.S. v. Deare:.

    Jeremiah Deare was indicted for conspiracy to engage in the business of dealing firearms without a federal firearms license in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(a)(1) and for making false statements with respect to records of licensed firearms dealers. Deare then filed a motion to dismiss the indictment, broadly challenging the constitutionality of § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements.

    Recent findings suggest that the district court denied his motion to dismiss, holding that federal licensing and record-keeping requirements are not implicated by the Second Amendment because such requirements do not affect an individual's right to keep or bear arms. The court further held that, even if federal licensing requirements are implicated by the Second Amendment, such requirements are consistent with our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation….

    Recent findings suggest that deare primarily challenges the district court's denial of his motion to dismiss the indictment. Specifically, he argues that the Second Amendment's plain text covers firearm sales, and that § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements are inconsistent with our Nation's history of firearm regulation.

    It has been revealed that the plain text of the Second Amendment covers the sale of firearms. As we noted in Reese v. BATFE (5th Cir. 2025), "the right to 'keep and bear arms' surely implies the right to purchase them." During oral argument, the government conceded that the Second Amendment applies to the commercial sale of firearms.

    Accordingly, we vacate the district court's order denying Deare's motion to dismiss the indictment and remand to the district court for further proceedings.

    (As I read the opinion, it doesn't affect the false statements charge.).

    Sources indicate that it's gratifying that our court today reaffirms what we should have long understood—that the Second Amendment right to "keep and bear Arms" plainly encompasses the sale of arms as well. It seems obvious that constitutional rights are meaningless if the Government can simply prohibit the means by which citizens are able to exercise those rights.

    Industry observers note that our dissenting colleague theorizes that 18 U.S.C. § 922(a) is not about constitutional rights, but about commercial regulation. It's the same view expressed by the district court below: "§ 922(a)(1) is a modest regulation of the commercial activity of selling/transferring firearms to others…. [F]ederal licensure and record keeping requirements do not affect an individual's rights to possess firearms…. [T]hese requirements affect only the seller. As such, Defendants have failed to persuade this Court that these commercial licensure and recordkeeping requirements implicate the Second Amendment.".

    Or as the dissent puts it simply, "the Second Amendment … doesn't mention sellers," so "I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered.".

    By that logic, the First Amendment doesn't mention sellers, so presumably booksellers aren't covered by the First Amendment, either. But that can't be right.

    Constitutional rights are constitutional rights, regardless of whether they're compensated—as I've noted on a number of occasions. And if that's true under the First Amendment, then it should be equally true in Second Amendment challenges to § 922(a) as well….

    It has been revealed that our dissenting colleague responds by offering a textual distinction between the First and Second Amendments. At bottom, the dissent theorizes that the "freedom of speech" contemplates sales, whereas "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms" does not. But with respect, I don't see the textual distinction that she sees. The theory is also hard to square with what we saw in Villarreal.….

    Judge Oldham, joined by Judge Ho, concurred in the judgment (though presumably they also joined their own unsigned opinion):.

    The first question presented is whether restrictions on the sale of firearms burden the Second Amendment rights of American citizens. They do—in at least two ways. First, such restrictions directly burden the seller's right to keep and bear arms. And second, they burden the prospective buyer's right to keep and bear arms, because the right to keep an item always includes the right to acquire it.

    Recent findings suggest that start with the constitutional text. The Second Amendment does not just prohibit the government from denying the right to keep and bear arms. Instead, it notes that the right cannot be "infringed." And at the Founding, "infringe" meant "violate," "destroy," or "hinder." Thus, the government cannot hinder the people's rights to keep and bear arms.

    Restrictions on sale hinder both the seller's and buyer's right to keep and bear arms. Start with the seller's right to possess firearms. The Second Amendment guarantees the right to keep guns for personal use, and the seller is an individual who can lawfully possess guns. And it's hornbook property law that the right to possess an article "includes the right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." So the right to keep a gun must include the right to dispose of that gun as the owner sees fit. This is not an independent "right to sell." Rather, my point is that governmental interference with the right to sell a firearm is itself a burden on the seller's existing property right in that firearm. It hinders and hence infringes the seller's rights.

    The same logic applies to the buyer. The buyer's ability to keep and bear arms is certainly "infringed" by regulations that hinder the purchase of arms. After all, the Supreme Court has explained that inherent in "property" is the "right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." In other words, a restriction on the sale of weapons obviously impacts the buyer's constitutional rights to acquire weapons. As one scholar has explained it:.

    According to recent reports, because one cannot 'keep' or 'bear' something without acquiring it, the act of acquiring arms must be included in the Second Amendment's 'right to keep and bear arms.' This is true for the same reason that the right to speak would be largely ineffective if it did not include the right to engage in financial transactions that are the incidents of its exercise. For there comes a point at which the regulation of action intimately and unavoidably connected with a right is a regulation of the right itself.

    Joseph G.S. Greenlee, The American Tradition of Self-Made Arms, 54 St. Mary's L.J. 35 (2023).

    This principle is not limited to the Second Amendment context. For example, consider the neighboring First Amendment. The Free Speech Clause "afford[s] the public access to discussion, debate, and the dissemination of information and ideas"—and thus clearly protects the right to sell and distribute speech, including speech written or produced by others. And it protects the recipient's right to receive information and ideas. Willis v. Town of Marshall (9th Cir. 2002) (Kozinski, J., concurring) ("[T]he right to hear and the right to speak are flip sides of the same coin."). Without a right to provide speech, there is no right to receive information and ideas.

    In a recent development, likewise, consider the Free Exercise Clause. "[T]he text of the Free Exercise Clause gives a specific group of people (those who wish to engage in the 'exercise of religion') the right to do so without hindrance." It is axiomatic that the right to free exercise of religion includes the right to practice it with others in, for example, houses of worship. Shutting down houses of worship is an obvious First Amendment violation for many reasons—not the least of which is that it prevents the faithful from communing with each other and with church leaders who provide teaching, holy sacraments, and other sacred traditions. Thus, the right to exercise religion includes a First Amendment freedom to participate in religious services with—and provide religious services to—others.

    These examples demonstrate clear principles. A right to property, free speech, corporate worship, and firearms includes the right to provide these things. And to acquire them….

    Judge Oldham also discussed the proper scope of a Fifth Circuit decision, U.S. v. Peterson (5th Cir. 2025) and concludes that it (1) "was wrong and should be overturned" and in any event (2) doesn't apply here; for more on that, read the full opinion.

    Judge Catharina Haynes dissented:.

    I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered by the Second Amendment (which doesn't mention sellers) …. {Second Amendment is quite different from the First Amendment mentioned in the concurrence. The First Amendment states "freedom of speech" and lists people in general which is quite large whereas the Second Amendment indicates "the right of people to keep and bear Arms" not mentioning selling Arms or all situations.}.

    [But] I am respectful of the majority opinion on that given our prior cases and what the government remarked. So, even assuming arguendo the sellers are covered, I see nothing in this case that highlights that the rules for the sellers in this context are inappropriate and, therefore, unconstitutional. Also, to me, since Deare did not properly challenge the relevant rules to show that they are abusive, I do not see a need to remand on that. To me, the relevant rules as to him are sufficient and proper, so I would simply affirm.

    I appreciate Judge Ho's and Judge Oldham's arguments that the right to keep and bear arms must include the right to acquire them, which in turn means that restrictions on sales must be evaluated to make sure they don't improperly burden the rights of would-be buyers. By way of analogy, the Court continues to recognize a right to use contraceptives (see Griswold v. Connecticut). Surely that must mean that a ban on selling contraceptives would unconstitutionally burden the would-be buyers' rights, and even less comprehensive restrictions on selling them might likewise be seen as too burdensome.

    According to recent reports, but I'm skeptical of the argument that the Second Amendment secures a right of sellers independent of the right of buyers. A bookseller may be said to be engaged in "speech" in the sense that conveying ideas to readers is a form of speech (including when one conveys them in exchange for money). A gun seller, on the other hand, isn't actually "keeping" a gun or "bearing" it. And though property rights do generally include the right to convey, including by sale, I don't think the Second Amendment should be seen as constitutionalizing that.

    By way of analogy, the law bans transferring guns to felons. That, the Court has said, is presumptively constitutional, because felons don't have the right to possess guns (focusing on the rights of the would-be gun possessor). But I don't think it follows that the law even implicates the right of gun sellers. When the law bans me from selling a gun to a felon, it isn't affecting my own ability to keep or bear the gun at all.

    Recent findings suggest that and this distinction between (1) the Second Amendment protecting gun sales as facilitative of the buyer's ability to have a gun, and (2) the Second Amendment gun sales as protecting the seller's own Second Amendment rights, may be practically significant. Under theory 1, there would likely be more room for regulation of sellers, since restrictions that only very modestly affect the buyer's ability to buy guns might then be viewed as presumptively constitutional. (That's consistent with D.C. v. Heller's statement that "nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on … laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms"). Under theory 2, there would be less room for regulation of sellers, since the sellers' own rights would be at stake as well.

    Again, that's also how the distinction might play out as to the right to use contraceptives, and how it played out as to abortion in the pre-Dobbs Roe/Casey era. For instance, the right to abortion was consistent with licensure requirements for people or organizations that perform abortions, so long as this didn't unduly interfere with women's ability to get abortions. Likewise, it seems to me, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms is consistent with licensure requirements for gun sellers, so long as it doesn't unduly interfere with people's ability to get guns that they can then keep and bear.

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1689 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that today, in Texas v.
    • The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.
    • Recent findings suggest that during the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that today, in Texas v. Blanche, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.

    The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.

    Recent findings suggest that during the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum. The House used this rule when passing the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (the Act), having mustered a quorum by counting hundreds of otherwise absent Members as present by proxy. The Senate then passed the bill, and the President signed it into law.

    The State of Texas argues that the House's proxy-presence rule is inconsistent with the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which would mean that the House did not validly pass the Act. See U.S. Const. art. I, § 5, cl. 1. Based on that proposition, Texas seeks injunctive relief against just one portion of the Act: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The federal Government responds that the enrolled-bill rule, which instructs that a bill's passage through the legislature is conclusive proof of its authenticity, precludes judicial review of whether the Act's passage complied with the Quorum Clause. Alternatively, the Government argues that the Quorum Clause permits proxy presence.

    The district court held that the enrolled-bill rule did not apply and that the House's passage of the Act—through use of the proxy-presence rule —violated the Quorum Clause. Accordingly, the district court enjoined the Government from enforcing the PWFA against Texas.

    We conclude that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review because Texas's constitutional challenge does not implicate a dispute of fact regarding the Act's passage. We further conclude that the Act's passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes—as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. "Proxy presence" does not count. While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause's constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat. We therefore affirm the judgment of the district court.

    The enrolled-bill doctrine articulated in Marshall Field does not preclude judicial review of Texas's Quorum Clause challenge. There are no disputed facts regarding the House's passage of the Act such that we would need to sift any extrinsic evidence. On the contrary, the parties agree that the House purportedly established a quorum only because it counted hundreds of proxies as "present." Texas's challenge therefore depends solely on the Quorum Clause's proper meaning.

    Through that lens, the House's passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 contravened the Quorum Clause. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and historical application all indicate that proxies may not be counted to establish a quorum. As the Supreme Court has held, and as Congress had previously done for over 230 years, Members must be present to satisfy the Quorum Clause. Presence-by-proxy does not suffice. An absent Member's assignment of his or her proxy cannot render that Member present for purposes of the Quorum Clause. Texas has carried its burden to show that it is entitled to a permanent injunction against the PWFA.

    Judge Graves wrote the dissent, joined by Judges Stewart, Richman, Southwick, Higginson, Douglas, and Ramirez. It begins:.

    In this suit, the State of Texas sought a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of one portion of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), attempting to veto Congress's protections for pregnant workers and upcoming parents while retaining millions in federal funding.

    On May 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted House Resolution 965, which authorized remote committee proceedings and remote voting in the House. Resolution 965 provides that:.

    1. [A]t any time after the Speaker . . . is notified . . . that a public health emergency due to a novel coronavirus is in effect, the Speaker . . . may designate a period . . . during which a Member who is designated by another Member as proxy in accordance with section 2 may cast the vote of such other Member or record the presence of such other Member in the House.

    Recent findings suggest that H.R. Res. 965 § 1(a), 116th Cong. (2020).

    Industry observers note that section 2 described the process for remote participation through designating proxies: the designating Member had to submit a signed letter to the Clerk that specified the designated Member. Id. § 2. Section 3 outlined the process for voting during covered periods, which, absent an extension, ran for forty-five days after the Speaker, or their designee, designated such a period. Id. §§ 1(b), 3. Section 4 authorized remote Committee proceedings. Id. § 4. Section 5 mandated that the chair of the Committee on House Administration certify that it would be feasible to use technology to conduct remote voting in the House, required that the chair of the Committee on Rules submit regulations providing for the implementation of remote voting, and provided for remote voting once those regulations were in place. Id. § 5. Section 6 required that Sections 1, 2, and 3 be carried out in accordance with existing House rules to the extent practicable. Id. § 6. During the 117th Congress, the House reaffirmed this practice in House Resolution 8 and continued to apply it. H.R. Res. 8 § 3(s), 117th Cong. (2021).

    At problem here: the House used these procedures as it voted on and passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. See 168 Cong. Rec. H10,529 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Under House rules, a quorum of the 435-Member House is a simple majority: 218. See, e.g., Rules of the House of Representatives, R. XX, cl. 6(b), H.R. Doc. No. 116-177, at 873–74 (2021). The vote on the final passage of the Act was 225 yeas, 201 nays, 1 "present," and 4 non-votes. 168 Cong. Rec. H10,528 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Out of the 431 votes, 205 votes were cast by Members in person and 226 were cast remotely by proxy. See id. at H10,529.

    In a recent development, even though less than a majority was physically present at the time of the vote, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Id. Representative Chip Roy of Texas, however, noted that a physical quorum was not present and reserved the right to object. Id. In response to a series of parliamentary inquiries from Representative Roy as to how a quorum was present, the Speaker Pro Tempore, Representative G.K. Butterfield, responded that a quorum was present because "Members casting their vote or recording their presence by proxy [we]re counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum" pursuant to House Resolution 8. Id.

    After the Act passed the House, presiding officers of both chambers of Congress printed and signed the bill. See 1 U.S.C. § 106. At that point, it was an "enrolled bill." Id. The enrolled bill was then sent to the President, who signed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 into law. See Pub. L. No. 117-328, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022).

    Sources indicate that the $1.7 trillion-dollar government funding bill was passed in accordance with House Rules, including House Resolution 8, which allowed members to record their presence remotely by proxy during the coronavirus pandemic. 431 votes were cast with respect to the bill. At the time, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Nonetheless, the State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause.

    According to recent reports, texas contends that the Act is invalid because the Quorum Clause required that a majority of Members be physically present on the House floor at the time of the vote. In so doing, Texas asks the courts to graft an additional requirement to the Quorum Clause of the Constitution.

    Sources indicate that I agree with the majority that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review of this particular constitutional challenge. However, I cannot agree with their addition of a new requirement to the Quorum Clause. Even though the majority declares that its reasoning is limited to the question of "whether the Quorum Clause allows proxy presence to be included in the quorum count," ante at 17–18, their conclusion is far more expansive. The conclusion that "[t]he Quorum Clause is concerned with physical presence" shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution. Ante at 28. Because the plain text of Article I, Section 5, Clause 1, historical practice, and evidence of the framers' intent all weigh against the addition of the majority's new "physical presence" requirement, I respectfully dissent.

    Judge Haynes did not join the dissent, but a footnote to the opinion reads:.

    Industry observers note that judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

    Although the majority purports to offer a narrow holding, and only blocks enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in Texas, the opinions rationale would provide a basis for invalidating everything else in the omnibus bill, which included everything from the ban on using TikTok on government devices to the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act.

    I doubt this decision will stand. I am not sure the Quorum Clause is justiciable, and I cannot see the Supreme Court upending all of the affected legislation on this basis.

    The petition for certiorari in this case writes itself. Another wild card is that the latest Attorney General of Texas may not press its case.

    More from Derek Muller on Election Law Blog.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname.

    It has been revealed that in a federal complaint filed Tuesday in the Southern District of New York, James mentioned he has been known as “Bron” since he was a young basketball standout in Ohio. He alleges that PlayVision and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, seek “to trade on” his “valuable name and reputation” by naming their app Bron.

    Recent findings suggest that there is no other connection between the word and the defendants or any other feature of their app, James alleges. He also argues in the complaint that when the defendants launched a marketing campaign for the Bron app earlier this month, they used a video advertisement that incorporated an artificial intelligence-generated version of him.

    Recent findings suggest that “The AI-generated version of Mr. James sits in an NBA-style locker room wearing a basketball jersey bearing Mr. James’s nickname, ‘Bron,’ above the number ‘23’—a number associated with Mr. James and the one he right now wears on the Philadelphia 76ers—with physical traits that mimic Mr. James, down to his identifiable tattoos,” according to the complaint.

    In a recent development, “Speaking in Mr. James’s voice, the AI-generated Mr. James scrolls through wagers on other NBA players in defendants’ Bron app,” the complaint continues. “The ad then urges viewers to ‘scroll to bet.’”.

    The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction preventing the defendants from using the “Bron” name; James’ name, image and likeness; and voice.

    Courthouse News Service has additional reporting.

    A representative for Bron did not respond to the publication’s request for comment.

    #32800. Tech Report: 5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1097 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: 5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living.
    • Recent findings suggest that there’s plenty of menace in small places.
    • Industry observers note that I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You expect danger in the city. Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living. Country intelligence has no succinct adjectives. Country-strong, that’s a thing. But, country-wise? More often than not, there is a misconception that life in the hinterlands will dull your edge, diminish your reflexes, lull you into a false sense of security.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s plenty of menace in small places. In towns with no interstate ramp, nameless desert stops with no cell phone service, a desperate farm community surrounded by an ocean of corn.

    Industry observers note that I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors. These don’t have to be set in the South—mine are—but they can happen anywhere. Maybe it’s Southern noir when done south of the Mason-Dixon line. Rural noir is a good name, and throws its arms around the whole genre, but it’s a mouthful. It comes out sounding slurry, even when I’m sober, and might not come out at all if I’ve had a cocktail. This subgenre of crime fiction goes by many names. I wish I could just tell people I wrote Southerns and have them understand—the way most people understand the Western. Till then, here are five of my favorite examples of novels that take place out past the last lights of town.

    Industry observers note that key note: I had to leave out a lot of authors I adore and beg you to read anything and everything by the following for outstanding examples of small-town, insular, tight-nit, and Sun-Belt crime: Flannery O’Connor, S.A. Cosby, Carson McCullers, Henry Wise, Attica Locke, Dennis Lehane, Megan Abbott, Ivy Pochoda, and Elmore Leonard. Please find them.

    Recent findings suggest that daniel Woodrell is incredible. I love every word he has ever written but Tomato Red is my favorite. It opens with a gorgeous run-on sentence that’s almost three hundred words long and, after reading it, it’s almost impossible not to collapse and read the whole book in one sitting. The novel’s hapless anti-hero, Sammy Barlach—recently fired from a dog food factory and fresh off a speed-fueled burglary attempt—throws in with siblings Jason and Jamalee Merridew. Jason, a local object of female obsession, and his sister Jamalee want to weaponize Jason’s beauty, blackmail wealthy woman, and get them both out of Venus Holler. Sammy hitches his wagon to the Merridew’s scheme. But for Jason, a gay man in the hills and hollows of the Ozarks, choosing to live an authentic life proves to me more dangerous than one of crime.

    It has been revealed that one of my favorite sayings from Tod Goldberg is that he writes about bad people doing terrible things to even worse people. In The Low Desert, he demonstrates this across twelve sometimes-connected stories set on the outskirts of California and Nevada. There are lonely deserts, fading resort towns, lost highways. Each story is a banger, but the fact that Goon Number Four isn’t your favorite TV show of the last decade is a miscarriage of justice. A story about a hired gun who enrolls in a community college, seeking to be rid of the life, only to find exploitation waiting in the halls of normalcy. The Low Desert has something I have never been able to fully articulate—feeling more like a great album, than the seminal work of crime fiction it is.

    According to recent reports, A personal favorite, Thompson’s Pop. 1280 is a novel that perfectly balances menace and comedy. Nick Corey, a terrible sheriff, oversees the 1280 souls of Potts County, Texas. Many of Nick’s constituents don’t want a sheriff, prefer to skirt the law, and tolerate him because he is pathologically shiftless. Our sheriff eats five meals a day, sleeps with any woman who’s up for it, sees murder as the only option rather than a last resort, and will do anything to keep his job. Not because he is ambitious, but because being sheriff allows him to do almost nothing. But, on the precipice of a difficult reelection, he reluctantly springs into action. Through the ensuing morass, Nick confronts sassy pimps, his pushy wife and her brother, his mistress and her husband, the town as whole, and the very concept of righteousness. Corey is a man who seems dumb, but isn’t. Someone dangerous and ruthless in the most peculiar and befuddling ways.

    Cormac McCarthy, No Country for Old Men.

    Recent findings suggest that cormac McCarthy’s most accessible novel. It is a literary crime novel that dissects the corrosive effects of money, heightened to break-neck entertainment by the inclusion of one of fiction’s most unforgettable bad dudes. In many ways, this is Anton Chigurh’s book the way Jaws belongs to the shark. Chigurh, a relentless hitman who’s as dangerous to his employers as he is to his targets, is evil with biblical scope. Ed-Tom Bell is a good man fading. A sheriff having and existential crisis, struggling to adapt to the requirements of his calling in a world where criminality has moved past opportunism and into something inconceivable. Throw in Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam vet who stumbles across two million dollars after a drug deal goes wrong, and you’re in for a ride. When Chigurh’s tide of malevolence come in. One man tries to stem it, the other retreats. Fates are decided by the flip of a coin.

    Frank Bill, Crimes in Southern Indiana.

    Industry observers note that frank Bill’s debut, Crimes in Southern Indiana, is a cold look at a brutal version of Indiana that exists off the interstates. Southern Indiana is an anomaly—not quite the South, not quite the Midwest. Claimed by none—like the folks Bill writes about. He drops seventeen stories about this distinct region across two hundred and seventy pages in an achingly authentic voice. He can do more damage in ten pages than most other savvy word-geeks could with a lifetime supply of paper. The Penance of Scoot McCutchen will wreck you. I think about it all the time.

    It has been revealed that ty Landers holds an MFA in Creative Writing and Writing for the Performing Arts from the University of California, Riverside. Born and raised in Alabama, he spent more than twenty years in Nashville, Tennessee, before moving to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with his wife and sons. His debut novel BABY QUEEN, out on November 17, 2026, is being adapted by HBO. For more on Ty Landers, visit: https://www.tylandersfiction.com/.

    #32797. Latest Update: Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (990 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media.
    • In a recent development, on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state.
    • “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media. Let alone the international news media. But during the traditionally slow Christmas holiday, when even serious outlets stoop to tracking Santa’s progress across the northern hemisphere and presenting expert commentary on decorations at the White House, the story about the bodies found in the backwoods of the Pacific Northwest arrived like a Christmas gift from News Kringle.

    In a recent development, on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state. After a three-day search that involved more than sixty volunteers from two states, dogs, drones, and helicopters working through harsh terrain, icy conditions, and a snowstorm, their frozen bodies were recovered. On December 28, Portland’s CBS television affiliate KOIN 6 was among the first to pick up the story.

    “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.

    Did someone say Sasquatch? Every editor in the world knew clickbait when they saw it. Within days, near-identical headlines appeared around the world, backed by the biggest names in news.

    CNN: 2 Oregon men die from exposure in a forest after they went out to look for Sasquatch.

    Fox News: 2 dead after search for Sasquatch in Washington national forest.

    NPR: 2 men were found dead from exposure after looking for Sasquatch.

    BBC: Two men found dead while searching for Bigfoot.

    Nine News Australia: Two men found dead in US after going on Christmas Eve hunt for Bigfoot.

    Hundreds, perhaps thousands, jumped in. The Associated Press. MSN. CBS News. HuffPost. Newsweek. Today. Yahoo News. USA Today. Newly introduced York Post. Los Angeles Times. San Francisco Chronicle. The Times. Daily Mail.

    The story was such a surefire traffic pusher that even specialized outlets ran with it. People. Sports Illustrated. AccuWeather. The celebrity and entertainment website TooFab. Spain’s national sports tabloid Marca. New Zealand’s Stuff. Taiwanese tabloid CTWant. The massively popular 52hrtt, a Chinese-language website that serves the global Chinese diaspora.

    There was no video, so each outlet looped the same images from a package of photos released by the Skamania County 23 sasquatch country Sheriff’s Office: four SAR volunteers on a snow-covered trail carrying an extension ladder through the forest; six volunteers in safety-orange jackets and helmets, one pointing a finger into the woods, using an extension ladder laid on the ground to cross a stream; a guy on hands and knees crawling across the ladder over a stream; a group of seven searchers using downed logs to cross a stream; and a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above an opening in the forest canopy.

    Recent findings suggest that in a digitally powered echo chamber, local, regional, national, and international outlets repeated the story almost word for word. All the way across the continent, News Center Maine television led its December 30 national news roundup in typical fashion:.

    In a recent development, we’ll start in Washington state. Two men were found dead there after going on a search for Bigfoot. They went out on their search a few days before Christmas Eve. When they didn’t return, family members contacted police. They were found after a three-day search. Local authorities there say it seems as though they likely died of exposure because of the weather conditions at the time and not being prepared.

    Sasquatch hunters. Christmas search. Poorly prepared. Died of exposure. That was all anyone seemed to know.

    Industry observers note that in fact, those elementary pieces of the story were all anyone in the news media actually did know. As even a cursory examination of the torrent of articles and broadcasts about the two bodies found in the forest revealed, the stories were noteworthy mostly for their striking uniformity and lack of information. But something about the story wasn’t right. Something didn’t add up.

    The rule that credible journalists are meant to follow is that the details in a story must support its headline—particularly if that headline makes an audacious claim. Two guys froze to death while looking for Bigfoot? Wow. Bring on the details.

    Industry observers note that but that was the thing about the story of the Christmas Sasquatch hunters. After the stun-gun heds and ledes, there were no details about the supposed Sasquatch hunt. Not scant details. Not vague details. No details whatsoever. As if by mandate, every outlet that picked up the story made sure to include Sasquatch in its headline and opening grab. Then they dropped the Bigfoot angle altogether.

    Recent findings suggest that how long had the men been out looking for Sasquatch? Did they have a track record as Sasquatch hunters? Were they carrying special equipment, such as video cameras, long-range microphones, or telephoto lenses? If they were out searching for Sasquatch in rugged terrain and winter conditions, why were they so ill prepared?

    On these and other questions related to the Sasquatch hunt teased in the headlines, every story was the same—strangely mute.

    Excerpted from Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the New American Wilderness by Chuck Thompson via Counterpoint Press.

    Recent findings suggest that chuck Thompson is the longtime editor of Columbia Insight, an award-winning environmental and outdoor news website based in Hood River, Oregon, just across the Columbia River from Skamania County and the Gifford Pinchot National Forest. A former executive producer with CNN.com, deputy editor of Men’s Journal, and Outside magazine contributor, he’s the author The Status Revolution: The Improbable Story of How the Lowbrow Became the Highbrow; the widely reviewed political screed Better Off Without ’Em: A Northern Manifesto for Southern Secession; the acclaimed travel memoir Smile When You’re Lying: Confessions of a Rogue Travel Writer; and Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the Newly introduced American Wilderness.

    • The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial problems was more of a First Amendment problem, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006. (Photo by Jeffrey M. Vinocur, CC-BY-SA-3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

    According to recent reports, the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Philadelphia mentioned Tuesday.

    The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial problems was more of a First Amendment problem, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.

    In her brief, Wax, a white Jewish woman, stated that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act prohibit discrimination “on the ground of race” and “on the basis of race,” respectively, differing them from Title VII.

    She argued that the the University of Pennsylvania had an alleged double standard, allowing faculty and students to participate in what she called antisemitic demonstrations against Israel without consequences but punishing her for her commentary on race.

    #32795. 5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1147 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted.
    • But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers.
    • Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted. It’s my eighth book. With each one I’ve taken a bigger, bolder, and yes, a more unhinged swing. And I’m not alone. There is a rabid pack of unhinged thriller writers out there, and we’re only getting more bananas.

    But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers. In fact, I’ve found it incredibly hard to whittle this list down to just five. This list bounces between the upcoming, the nearly new and the really rather old.

    Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

    Industry observers note that one of those novels so powerful that it becomes a conceptual byword (by-phrase?) used even by people who have never read it. Published in 1886 and so brisk it’s actually a novella, this unflinching gothic masterpiece still holds its own in 2026.

    There is almost as much mythology about the writing of the book as is contained in its pages. Stevenson claimed that it sprang from a wild nightmare that contained three scenes and the central idea, “of a voluntary change becoming involuntary.” His step-son claimed it was written in a three-day fit of pique. His wife claimed that Stephenson burned the first version after she suggested he was writing an allegory, which riled him up before he realized he agreed, and then started again.

    Stephenson’s health at the time was dire, he was on medication to stop his lungs hemorrhaging, which could have stimulated the originating nightmare. According to some rumors he was also taking cocaine, which could also explain the mad work rate and agitation….

    If you haven’t read it recently (or perhaps ever), you may raise an eyebrow at its inclusion in a list of thrillers but it more than earns its place.

    We have unreliable characters, memory blackouts, dual personalities and a race to stop a killer. And it’s actually, I would argue, a speculative thriller given that the whole problem starts with Dr Jekyll experimenting to create a serum that can overcome the dark parts of his personality. Instead, the serum splits him into two—the good Dr Jekyll, and the evil Mr Hyde.

    Sarah Pinborough, Behind Her Eyes.

    I know this came out nearly ten years ago but I’m still agape at its twists. Sarah Pinborough tore up the rule book with this one, and proved that you could still find fresh ways to shock a savvy audience of thriller readers.

    Sources indicate that if you’ve not read it, I don’t want to give anything away but what starts as a tense psychological thriller about a single mum having an affair with her boss while forming a close friendship with the boss’s wife, soon takes a hard swerve into lucid dreaming, astral projection and a past timeline exploring trauma and mental illness. And if that sounds heavy and gloomy, I’m doing it a massive disservice because it is an absolute rollercoaster.

    The ending was so WILD that it was a key part of the marketing, with the hashtag #WTFthatending spreading through Book Twitter (this was 2017, after all…).

    Lisa Jewell, None Of This Is True.

    According to recent reports, as a long-term fan, I loved watching the queen of women’s fiction become the doyenne of domestic suspense before winding her way down an ever-darker garden path. But Lisa Jewell’s 2023 novel, None Of This Is True, was a real escalation.

    Industry observers note that A fever dream of lies, paranoia and platonic limerence. Alix is a successful true crime podcaster who meets her “birthday twin,” Josie, an unassuming local woman born on the same day but whose life is very different.

    According to recent reports, they both have secrets, of course, which I’m loathe to give away but the novel is unflinching around dark topics like grooming, alcoholism and family dysfunction. For all its sucker punches (and the twists are *brain exploding emoji*) this is a nuanced and heartfelt exploration of the stories we tell ourselves in order to survive.

    Industry observers note that if you were an unemployed gambling addict unable to pay your debts and whose loved ones were being threatened by the Yakuza, you’d take the first well-paid job that comes your way too, right? In this case, as a private chef to a reclusive billionaire in remote Japan.

    Soon, protagonist Ed is somewhat learning on the job in the best kitchen money can buy at the heart of an enormous mansion, with an endless supply of whatever ingredients the esoteric tastes of his boss desires….

    It’s been likened to Butter by Asako Yuzuki and there are overlaps in themes of greed, obsession and—of course—murder, but while Butter is a slow burn, Greedy is a runaway train. Messy, freaky and eye wateringly gory. I mean all those things as compliments!

    Fiona Cummins, Serial Killer Survivors Club.

    While 1980s teenager Robyn reels from the discovery that her father was a serial killer, her life is made infinitely worse by community ostracism and judgement.

    An experimental therapy group for the familial survivors of murderers changes her life, finally giving her the acceptance and friendship she has always craved. But when one of her new friends disappears in a town where three other young women are already missing, Robyn and her found-family risk everything to find them. After all, with their intimate knowledge of killers, the Serial Killer Survivors Club are the best hope these missing women have….

    According to recent reports, I pat myself on the back for my ability to predict twists but this one spun me for a total loop. I was lucky enough to grab an advanced readers copy of this, which will be published next year in the UK and US. I highly recommend pre-ordering.

    My own unhinged thriller, The Sleeper, follows librarian Maya who falls asleep on a sleeper train and wakes up in a version of the world where history has changed overnight, her own life has been erased and nobody remembers her.

    And the version of Britain she’s now living in? Just saying the wrong things can put you in the crosshairs of the state. Which is a massive problem for Maya, who in her bewilderment, has asked way too many questions already….

    Industry observers note that holly Seddon is the author of several thrillers, including the international bestseller Try Not to Breathe, The Hit List, and 59 Minutes. After growing up in the English countryside obsessed with music and books, Holly worked in London as a journalist and editor. After several years in Amsterdam, she now lives in Kent with her family and writes full time. Find out more at HollySeddon.com.

    #32792. Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2220 w)

    Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2220 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, tuscany, 1972.
    • When Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray.
    • It has been revealed that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful fresh novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, tuscany, 1972. Bardo Sacchetti has the people of the Val di Cornia wrapped around his little finger. Thanks to him and his band of tomb raiders, locals in the impoverished region can now buy fridges for their homes or give their kids an education. He asks for nothing in return except for gratitude.

    When Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray. Former alliances fall apart and Bardo’s empire looks like it might be destroyed by violence. Veleno has some massive decisions to make.

    It has been revealed that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful fresh novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis. The story unfolds from their perspectives.

    I sent written questions to Naspini, and Edoardo Andreoni translated his written responses from Italian into English. The interview has been edited for length.

    Radha Vatsal: Let’s start with some background. Tuscany, where the novel takes place, seems to be littered with antiquities. Is this more the case in Tuscany than in other parts of Italy? Can you describe some of the types of antiquities that have been found there in recent years?

    According to recent reports, sacha Naspini: Actually, that’s true of pretty much all of Italy. It’s a country where history has accumulated over millennia, layer upon layer. Here, even a routine excavation can turn into an archaeological discovery.

    Tuscany is no exception. In fact, it’s one of the regions where this historical layering is particularly evident, largely thanks to the Etruscan civilization, which preceded Roman rule. Discoveries are still being made today. Take the recent finds at San Casciano dei Bagni, near Siena: extraordinary bronzes, along with coins, crowns, jewelry, votive arms and heads….

    It has been revealed that as for The Witch’s Mouth, the novel is set in a specific part of Tuscany, the Val di Cornia. It’s an area I know well, one that plays an important role in the fictional universe of some of my novels. This was once home to Populonia, one of the most important Etruscan cities and the only one built directly on the coast. In the Gulf of Baratti, you can visit Etruscan necropolises, monumental tombs, burial chambers carved into the rock, and the remains of Etruscan and Roman settlements.

    RV: The events in the novel occur in the early 1970s. Was there a particular reason for choosing this time period?

    Recent findings suggest that SN: Yes, there is. Choosing this period was an exciting challenge, and one that felt necessary. The Witch’s Mouth was born out of long conversations with tomb raiders and smugglers who were active during that time. Suddenly I came across some truly extraordinary, almost unbelievable stories. That’s when I began thinking about using this material as the basis for a novel.

    There were also three aspects that I found particularly fascinating. First of all, the “fever” I always noticed in the people who told me about their adventures. That’s the expression they would use: “digging fever.” It went beyond money or swashbuckling adventure—a special light would sparkle in their eyes. As these small-town Indiana Jones recalled those times, that almost addictive excitement was rekindled— the excitement of the moment when, after devising a plan, they would finally manage to break into a burial site, the first people to set foot there in millennia. And then reach out and touch the objects… Part of my job was to try to capture their passion.

    It has been revealed that the second aspect was even more intriguing and had to do specifically with the Val di Cornia. The trafficking of archaeological artifacts was already underway in other parts of Italy—for instance in the Tuscia region—but in this small corner of Tuscany, people were late to the game.

    It has been revealed that I heard crazy stories of farmers whose cellars were filled with bronzes that had turned up when they were plowing the land, and who would give them to their grandchildren to play with, like toy soldiers. After storms at sea, amphorae would wash up on the shore at Baratti. Kids would place them on top of low walls and throw rocks at them. Women would show up at Mass on Sunday wearing earrings and necklaces found in the fields….

    So I wondered, what would happen if an entire community, largely made up of people who struggle to make ends meet, suddenly realized that their homes were full of objects they considered worthless but that could fetch millions on the black market?

    Sources indicate that as I was researching the historical archives of the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, I came across a news story from 1971 about a twelve-inch bronze artifact seized by the Carabinieri. It was about to be sold to an American collector for half a billion lire (roughly $5 million in today’s money). People in that region had piles of similar bronzes, tossed aside in a corner.

    It has been revealed that finally, a purely personal aspect. I spent part of my childhood and adolescence in that region. Other kids and I would form our own little gangs and sneak out of the house in the middle of the night armed, with ropes, shovels, and spades, and head off into the woods. We imagined we were living in The Goonies, but instead of searching for One-Eyed Willy’s treasure, we were searching for Etruscan artifacts. Thinking back on it, what mattered wasn’t so much finding something as the adventure itself. Entering the woods at night was a significant challenge. And then the thrill of digging, without really knowing where to look… In a way, I think I experienced some of that same fever the “professional” tomb raiders talked about.

    RV: The Witch’s Mouth is an ensemble novel with a lot of different characters, but it revolves around Bardo. He’s almost a godfather-type figure in the way he involves so many different kinds of people in his activities and spreads the wealth he earns. Tell us about your inspiration for creating him.

    SN: Everything that happens in the novel is inspired by the interviews I mentioned earlier. But the characters are entirely the product of my imagination, as are the main plot and the various subplots.

    According to recent reports, when it comes to Bardo, I did a little “plundering” myself. Based on the stories I heard, I imagined this guy who, even as a kid, recognized the value of these artifacts, which everyone else treated like useless old junk taking up space.

    Recent findings suggest that but Bardo is also a man of action, and a pretty clever one. He knows how hard life is for the families of Populonia. He starts getting them to hand over their “pieces,” as they call them in the trade, and then sells them to the more experienced tomb raiders in the Tuscia region, returning with the money. Real money, not a few pennies.

    Industry observers note that before long, everyone starts looking at Bardo like a sort of saint. Everyone is knocking on his door with an artifact in their hand. And Bardo is extremely good at weaving a network built on trust and gratitude. That means protection—Bardo is untouchable. This is something else that fascinated me: at least in the beginning, there wasn’t a gun in sight. But then the operation grows exponentially. Billions of lire start pouring in. And where there’s that much money, guns usually follow.

    RV: Of the novel’s many great characters, I was fascinated by Elisa, Bardo’s wife; Silvana, the prostitute; and the Marquis. As you write, do you have favorites? Do some of the characters come more easily to you than others?

    Recent findings suggest that SN: Obviously I love them all, not only because of the role they each play in the story—a character is always an opportunity to explore different points of view, different lives and legacies… What I mean is, how does a particular character, with their own history, react to certain events? That’s part of the magic of writing. Especially when we explore uncomfortable aspects of human nature and relationships.

    According to recent reports, that remarked, among the characters you mentioned, Silvana and the Marchese have a special place in my heart. Silvana truly is the queen (I should say, the Principessa) of the novel. The Marchese, for his part, embodies a desperation that is part of the landscape and is compounded by his broken dreams, a desperation that still moves me. Although in the end… but I’d better stop here.

    RV: In many ways, this is the story of a gang of tomb robbers but it’s also the story of an ecosystem of stolen goods and people.

    SN: I had some interesting experiences in this respect during the promotion of the book in Italy. Together with my Italian publishers, we had the wonderful idea of organizing some events in archaeological museums. Some of the events were fantastic. In other cases, though, for instance in Vetulonia, the director of the magnificent local museum declined to participate. He didn’t want to celebrate, right in a place designed to house Etruscan artifacts, a story about thieves who had deprived everyone of the opportunity to admire works of art and experience the sense of connection we can feel with the people who lived in distant times.

    But I’m not an educator; I’m a novelist. I try to make sense of the world through stories. Even if these stories are unsettling—in fact, all the better. What I’m saying is, “Hey, look, this happened too.” I’m saying, “Hey, look at how these people lived. How they reacted, what they dreamt about, what circumstances led them to make certain choices.” And I know very well that it’s wrong to prevent the public from viewing a work of art, locking it away instead in some billionaire’s safe.

    I’ll go further. For me, the real damage inflicted by tomb raiders is not the sale of a particular artifact to a private collector. The real theft—and maybe it’s the novelist in me talking—has to do with removing a clue (the artifact itself) from the place where it was found, thereby interrupting a story. Otherwise, archaeologists would be able to tell us how people loved, what clothes they wore or what food they ate, what gods they worshipped, what stories they passed down in that very place. This is what they rob us of, to make a few million dollars. I hope that somehow, between the lines of my novel, this message comes across. But according to some museum directors, I’ve missed the mark.

    RV: Are there other novels or writers you draw inspiration from in your work?

    SN: The list would be endless, stretching from my formative years to the present, now that I’ve just turned fifty. It would comprise all the different kinds of writing I’ve sought out, explored, and measured myself against. And yet I feel like I’m just starting out.

    To mention some writers that have a place in my heart, in no particular order: Italo Calvino, Stephen King, Albert Camus, Joyce Carol Oates, John Steinbeck, Chuck Palahniuk, Beppe Fenoglio, Ágota Kristóf, Mikhail Bulgakov. If you asked me again a minute from now, the list would be completely different. I’m thinking of John Fante, or the fantasy novels I adored as a teenager. And what about Dumas and his Count of Monte Cristo?

    Seriously, I never know how to answer this question. But I think that each of these writers has given me a great gift: they “gave me permission” to be brave. To let my imagination spill onto the page, for what it’s worth. And all the voices that come with it.

    RV: What are you reading and/or working on at the moment?

    Recent findings suggest that SN: On my nightstand are books by David Szalay and Ernest Jünger—the latter a special gift I received, a book that I’ve already read but want to reread. Recently, I returned to John Fante’s Wait Until Spring, Bandini after many years—what a knockout. I don’t think it will ever get old. I also really loved Tiffany McDaniel’s The Summer That Melted Everything.

    Sources indicate that on my computer is a novel forthcoming in Italy, Il ronzio (“The Buzzing”), which is in the final stages of editing. Of course, I’m also working on another novel. And I’m having fun writing the treatment for a TV series, which is due soon. And listen to this: after twenty years of writing books, for the first time ever, there’s a police inspector in one of my stories. I never would have imagined it.

    Radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The Upcoming York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

    Uscreen is the video monetization platform for businesses building recurring revenue from video content. Our customers replace a patchwork stack of separate hosting, community, courses, email, and app vendors with one branded experience across web, mobile, and TV.

    In a recent development, the platform is only half of it. We believe growth requires behavior, not just software. Customers don't stall because a feature is missing. They stall because they priced wrong, never built an email list, or rolled out an offer nobody wanted. Coaching is how we fix that, and it's part of the product rather than an add-on.

    You own a segment, and you run it like a growth marketer.

    Sources indicate that we have a cohort of smaller video businesses where retention is not where it should be. Nobody owns it today. You will. The revenue that stays in that segment, and the revenue that grows inside it, is yours.

    It has been revealed that this is a coaching role for someone with a growth marketer's mindset. We wouldn't hire a demand gen marketer who couldn't analyze the state of the business and figure out what's needed, and we won't hire a coach who can't either. You'll look at a customer's business the way an owner would: where the revenue comes from, where it leaks, and what to do next. You pull your own numbers to get there. When a customer needs a custom report to answer a growth question, you build it yourself.

    It has been revealed that it's a one-to-many job. Your cohort is larger than a 1:1 book, so the work is designing coaching that scales: cohort programs, group sessions, office hours, and triggered outreach when the data claims a business is drifting. You'll build that motion rather than inherit it.

    Success is measured in dollars: gross revenue retention in your cohort first, expansion second. Not tickets closed, not calls booked.

    It has been revealed that A coach with a growth marketer's mindset. Maybe you've run growth or demand gen for a small business, built your own audience, or coached founders through their numbers. You understand how a membership business makes money, you pull your own analytics to see what's working, and you're comfortable doing it in front of a client.     Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that there’s a whole new wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases.
    • Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting.
    • Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that there’s a whole new wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases. Before I get to the recommendations, you may be wondering: what time period exactly are we talking? For the purposes of this article, the medieval era is roughly defined as between 1000-1500, depending on where the characters live. For example: 15th century Italy = Renaissance. 15th century Estonia = Medieval. Burgundy, I suppose, is half and half. Periodization is a continuum much more than a series of hard stops and new beginnings, and the Renaissance is just the Middle Ages with better marketing (see Inventing the Renaissance for more on the debate).

    Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting. Most are new releases from this year or next year, but there are two older titles that are still recent enough to count for this trend. Books that are not yet published have their publication dates next to their publisher info. If you’ve got any Dark Ages-set mysteries to recommend to me, please comment, because I would very much like to read them.

    Recent findings suggest that M. T. Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.

    Industry observers note that this came out in 2024, which I consider recent enough to include as part of this trend piece—especially when considering a medieval time scale. Also it’s awesome. In Nicked, a group of disparate travelers sets off on an odyssey of the medieval world with a common 11th century mission: they’ve been hired to steal the Anatolian relics of a powerful saint and transport them to an Italian city state in hopes of sparking more commerce from pilgrims (the medieval equivalent of taking the Dodgers from Brooklyn to LA). Along the way, they form deep bonds, some blossoming into romance, and take in the sights and sounds of the entire Mediterranean world. M. T. Anderson does that rare feat of capturing the spirit of the time, granting readers a lively, Rabelaisian interpretation of an unfairly maligned era (see history book The Bright Ages for further appreciation).

    Paul Brous, The Undying Lamb (Rising Action) Setting: Italian states, 1230.

    When a book starts with a glossary featuring words from several now-dead languages, you just know that it’s going to be impeccably researched. In Paul Brous’ medieval-set thriller, an Albigensian assassin and an English knight must protect a child with an inconvenient lineage, as a vast array of forces attempt to eliminate their vulnerable charge. Perfect for those who enjoyed Conclave, but wish it had been set waaaay further back in history.

    James Bennett, Mother of Night (Evil Twin, March 2027) Setting: Holy Roman Empire, 1291.

    In this intense work of historical horror, Saladin’s victories have sent a ragged group of crusaders fleeing from the Holy Land, their only option to board a rickety vessel soon enough broken by stormy seas. Shipwrecked and far from home, the few survivors find succor and strangeness amongst a group of miserable swamp-dwellers who warn of danger ahead; the crusaders, determined to forge ahead, do not listen, with predictably dire consequences and a surprising amount of singing.

    Ferdia Lennon, Brother Nothing (Holt, June 2027) Setting: France, 1369.

    In a recent development, set just a decade before the events of Doom Painting, Brother Nothing follows a newly appointed provost and his precociously intelligent daughter as they flee plague-ridden Paris for a town in the North of France. While their new abode does appear safe from pestilence, other dangers are many, including the perennial threat of English soldiers, an epidemic of children gone missing, and a murder pinned on a prodigal son who confesses to every possible crime— save the crime of which he is accused. As the provost uncovers layer after layer of shocking crimes and terrifying cover-ups, he and his few allies begin to suspect the entire town of conspiracy, for what reads a bit like Red Harvest, medieval style.

    Sources indicate that A.K. Blakemore, Doom Painting (Scribner, April 2027) Setting: England, 1381.

    Industry observers note that I have complete trust in A.K. Blakemore’s power to render historical fiction as vivid and complex as depictions of the present, and her new novel of the English Peasant’s Revolt does not disappoint. In 1381, England’s most oppressed rose up against the conditions of their serfdom, driven to rebellion by the devastation of the plague and the endless war with France. For 16 days, they challenged the notion that some should rule while others serve, embodied by Wat Tyler’s epic call-to-arms: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman?” As a side note, I’ve been planning to get a tattoo of that slogan in Ye Olde Englishe font for a while now, so maybe it’s time to bite the bullet. Also the book confirms what I have always known: Wat Tyler had major sex appeal.

    Indrek Hargla, The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press) Setting: 15th Century Tallinn.

    Recent findings suggest that indrek Hargla’s tale of a crime-solving apothecary is based in obscure, and very real, history; the mystery unraveled by the amateur sleuth takes its jumping off point from a mysterious note in Latvian historical records, for a richly detailed and vividly imagined take on a high-water mark in Latvia’s regional influence. In The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church, the murder of an aging knight leads a city luminary towards a horrifying secret with deep implications for the city’s fragile economic status and unstable power structure.

    Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street (Pushkin Press) Setting: Estonia, 1419.

    In a recent development, hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

    Jo Harkin, The Pretender Setting: England, Ireland, Burgundy, 15th Century.

    Sources indicate that at the tail end of the Wars of the Roses, an ordinary farm boy is plucked from his simple village life and trained up to become a king. He’s been swapped for a commoner at birth by his dead Earl of a father and forgotten about in the midst of internecine warfare; now, he’s the last hope for the house of York to triumph over its Tudor rivals. But does he have the stuff it takes to fight through his own doubts and become king? And will he survive the endless sacrifices demanded in his ascent to the throne? This is an excellent book to help you understand the inspirations behind Game of Thrones, or the power politics of Elaine’s kingdom in Wheel of Time.

    Katherine Arden, The Unicorn Hunter (Del Rey) Setting: Brittany, Late 15th Century.

    In 15th century Brittany, a noblewoman facing an unwanted union with a far-away lord puts in motion a clever plan to hold off the wedding: her husband-to-be must join her in a unicorn hunt in the dense, dark forest near to her castle. Soon, they find themselves transported into a magical realm beset by an ancient curse that only the lady and her wooing courtiers can break. The Unicorn Hunter takes its inspiration from the real Anne of Brittany, whose marriage to the King of France was just another method of preserving what little sovereignty her province could hold onto under the steady creep of French imperial influence, and who brought two beds to her wedding as a symbol of her independence. I think I would have quite liked Anne of Brittany—Katharine Arden certainly feels a sprightly kinship with the impish aristocrat.

    According to recent reports, molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

    Industry observers note that A former Motley Rice attorney was sentenced Monday in Charleston, South Carolina, to 87 months in prison and ordered to pay more than $2.5 million in restitution. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A former Motley Rice attorney was sentenced Monday in Charleston, South Carolina, to 87 months in prison and ordered to pay more than $2.5 million in restitution for defrauding the law firm through fictitious companies and ‌false settlement claims.

    William Christopher Swett, 42, had previously pleaded guilty to four counts of ​wire fraud and four counts of money laundering, according to a story by Reuters.

    A lawyer ​at South Carolina-based ⁠Motley Rice for 12 years, Swett had a severe gambling addiction and substance abuse issues, according to court papers filed on his behalf.

    Prosecutors have alleged that Swett profited for years ⁠by creating fictitious legal services companies that received reimbursements from Motley Rice. In addition, he allegedly filed fake personal injury claims for family members and put the proceeds into bank accounts that he controlled.

    As longtime CrimeReads readers (“CrimeReaders”) know, the editors of this website are always interested in news related to the Loch Ness Monster. Especially me. For example, several years ago, I wrote about how, in 2016, a bunch of Norwegian scientists had sent a high-tech robot down into Loch Ness to scan the, and the robot sent back sonar scans of a creature that looked exactly like the Loch Ness monster, but actually, it turned out to be a model of the Loch Ness Monster built for the 1969 film The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes that had accidentally sunk during filming. So that was a bummer. A HILARIOUS bummer, but a bummer nonetheless.

    Sources indicate that any Loch Ness Monster-related news intrigues me. So you can imagine my delight when I came across news of an upcoming series from the BBC and BritBox. It’s called The Loch Ness Mysteries.

    It’s set near Loch Ness, obviously, and it’s about a young, irascible, beautiful London detective who winds up being kicked out (I think?) of her job, only to wind up investigating a personal matter near Inverness… and being drawn into a strange mystery near Loch Ness.

    So, in the words of the genius who wrote the BBC’s press release, “from Scotland Yard to Scotland Scotland.”.

    According to recent reports, also, what’s the beautiful, brilliant, difficult detective’s name? DCI Vanessa “Nessie” Keen.

    It has been revealed that the series will star Melissa George, Jamie Sives, and Ashley Storrie, and will be six episodes long. Ed Sellek of Sister Boniface Mysteries is the creator and head writer.

    Filming begins before the end of the year, so stay tuned!
